solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Shrivel up in the company of Her Majesty

parts.note: to be in someone's company is to be with them
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword shorthand for the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone wilting from boredom while attending the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that dry out and shrink are said to droop and fade in this way, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Know-all from Wisconsin, the main source of controversy over scripture

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece over another comes above it

parts.note: WI is the postal abbreviation for Wisconsin
the main is an old poetic name for the open sea

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject once called scripture

explanation.surface: A smug Wisconsin pundit stirring up religious controversy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' means the sea. RE (religious education) is a British school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart aleck who thinks they know everything is the mocking sense of this old word.

clue.text: Hinged flap in cross-section, seen from below

indicators.note: in a down clue, viewing from the bottom upward reads the letters in reverse

parts.note: a rood is a cross or crucifix
a part is a section

explanation.surface: A cutaway diagram of a hinged panel, viewed from underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross-section' looks like one technical term, but it splits into two words. A rood is the cross in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged panel set in a floor or ceiling is exactly this kind of flap.

clue.text: European left supporting call for canine protection?

indicators.note: in a down clue, a supporting piece sits below the others

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A European politician backing a campaign to protect dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canine' suggests dogs but means canine teeth, which this coating protects.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard outer layer of a tooth shields it, including the pointed canines.

clue.text: OAPs regularly left huge amounts of money for animals

indicators.note: taking every other letter of the pensioners' abbreviation leaves its first and third letters

parts.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize, very large
sums are amounts of cash

explanation.surface: Pensioners bequeathed vast fortunes to their pets.
explanation.walkthrough: OAPs are old-age pensioners in Britain; 'regularly left' keeps O and P. OS (outsize) is a clothing-label size.
explanation.definitionFit: These American marsupials are a kind of creature, so the plural fits the general word for beasts.

clue.text: Spot sanctimonious politician with lingerie inside out

parts.note: pi is short for pious, sanctimonious
an MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: with the inside taken out only the outer letters remain

explanation.surface: Catching a pious politician wearing his underwear inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside out' looks like a garment on wrongly, but means the inside of 'lingerie' is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A small inflamed bump on the skin is a common British synonym for a spot.

clue.text: Shivering Sherpa is angel of the highest order

indicators.note: shivering shakes something, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A cold Himalayan guide is a saint of the highest rank.
explanation.walkthrough: A Sherpa is a Himalayan mountain guide.
explanation.definitionFit: In traditional angelology these six-winged beings rank first of the nine choirs of angels.

clue.text: Open University don neglecting to study mammal

indicators.note: neglecting to do something leaves it out

parts.note: to do a subject is to study it
a seal is a marine mammal

explanation.surface: An Open University lecturer too busy to research marine mammals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open University' looks like the British distance-learning body, but 'Open' is the definition. DON losing DO (study) leaves N.
explanation.definitionFit: To break the seal on a letter or package is to open it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Carpet in Chartres Cathedral

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow

explanation.surface: A rug lying in a French cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a floor covering but is the verb meaning to scold severely.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to reprimand them harshly; the old verb means to criticise scornfully.

clue.text: Article on fake witch doctor

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it

parts.note: a sham is a fake or fraud
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece exposing a bogus witch doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper story, but it is the grammatical article AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribal healer believed to reach the spirit world is the figure meant; the two terms are near synonyms.

clue.text: In the morning siblings bring back fine food for Olympians

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning hours
bros is short for brothers

indicators.note: to bring something back is to send it the other way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, with the digit 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Brothers and sisters bringing breakfast for athletes at the Games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympians' suggests athletes, but means the gods of Mount Olympus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the gods on Mount Olympus ate this, which kept them immortal.

clue.text: Befuddled dad randomly ran off, scratching head

indicators.note: letters put in a random order are rearranged
scratching out the head removes the first letter

parts.note: someone who fled ran off

explanation.surface: A confused father bolted at random, rubbing his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'randomly' rearranges DAD to ADD; 'scratching head' drops the F of FLED.
explanation.definitionFit: A muddled brain is described with this word, as if scrambled like a rotten egg.

clue.text: Rebellious Roman poet shunning chap, the sod

indicators.note: a rebellious thing is revolting, turning over, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: Ovid was a Roman poet

indicators.note: shunning something keeps it out

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a chap

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a disobedient poet who ignores a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sod' looks like an insult, but sod is a piece of turf.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of turf gouged out by a golf club is a small chunk of grass and earth.

clue.text: Careless husband follows pathetic chums back

indicators.note: one piece following another comes after it
read back means read in reverse order

parts.note: something pathetic is sad
chums are pals

explanation.surface: A careless spouse trailing after some sorry friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses SADPALS to SLAPDAS, and the H of husband comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hasty and sloppy work is done without care, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Dog biting backside of irksome individual

parts.note: biting and sharp both mean cutting or keen

indicators.note: the backside is the rear, the last letter

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one, an individual

explanation.surface: A dog biting the backside of an annoying person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biting' looks like what the dog does but means sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: This wrinkled Chinese breed is a kind of hound.

clue.text: Supple movement of snake shedding skin

indicators.note: losing the skin removes the outer letters of the word

parts.note: a snake moves with a gliding slither

explanation.surface: A snake gliding gracefully as it sloughs its skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shedding skin' removes the S and R on the outside of SLITHER.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a body that bends easily and moves with grace.

clue.text: Debauchery leads to rheumatism in old timers

indicators.note: the leading letters of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A doctor warning that wild living gives elderly people joint pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' takes the first letters of 'rheumatism in old timers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild, unrestrained revelry or dissipation is an older sense of the word, as in running wild.

clue.text: Heavenly body of setter in bed

indicators.note: one piece in another goes inside it

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
the crossword setter refers to themselves as me

explanation.surface: A beautiful body, the setter's own, lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' hints at a beautiful figure, but means a celestial object.
explanation.definitionFit: An icy object with a glowing tail orbiting the sun is a celestial body.

clue.text: The smell of us is hidden by case of Bulgarian whiskey

indicators.note: one thing hidden by another is covered by it, so it goes inside
the case of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: our means belonging to us
BO is body odour, an unpleasant smell

explanation.surface: Our body odour is disguised by a case of Bulgarian spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The smell of us' reads as ours, so the possessive comes first. Bourbon is spelt whiskey because it is American.
explanation.definitionFit: This American spirit is distilled mainly from corn and is one kind of the drink.

clue.text: Question posh priest masquerading as comic

parts.note: U means upper-class, posh

indicators.note: masquerading means in disguise, so the letters appear in a new order

explanation.surface: Asking whether a grand cleric in disguise is really a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a British usage made famous by Nancy Mitford.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes witty jokes is a comic or wit, so the two nouns match.

clue.text: Mates who messed about a bit

indicators.note: letters messed about are rearranged

explanation.surface: Friends who fooled around for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit' looks like a stretch of time, but is the adverb meaning to some degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions mean to a small degree or slightly, as in rather tired.

clue.text: Periodically debug room in zone's capital

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: Sweeping a room for bugs from time to time in a city's security zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' takes the even letters of 'debug room'. The definition is cryptic: the zone is the eurozone and capital means money.
explanation.definitionFit: The single currency is the money used throughout the eurozone, so it is that zone's capital.

clue.text: Force Brownie to turn up for charity event

parts.note: the RAF is the Royal Air Force

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up reads the letters from the bottom, in reverse

parts.note: a brownie is a helpful sprite in folklore, like an elf

explanation.surface: Pressing a Brownie to appear at a fundraiser.
explanation.walkthrough: A Brownie is a young Girl Guide, but here the folklore sprite. RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Charities often raise money by selling tickets for a prize draw.

clue.text: Gangs of disheartened adults

indicators.note: losing the heart removes the middle letters

parts.note: adults are grown-ups

explanation.surface: Gangs made up of dispirited adults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' removes the middle two letters, W and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Bands or sets of people are collections, a plural synonym.

clue.text: Missing last rally, excluding learner drivers

indicators.note: excluding means leaving out

parts.note: L is the learner plate in Britain; several drivers give several L letters

explanation.surface: Learner drivers left out of the final car rally.
explanation.walkthrough: British learner drivers display L-plates; the three Ls are removed from 'last rally'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has gone off course and is lost is missing.

clue.text: Poles embracing woman in prime

indicators.note: one piece embracing another holds it inside

parts.note: S and N are the south and north poles
Eve is the first woman in the Bible

explanation.surface: Men from Poland hugging a woman in the prime of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like Polish people but means the north and south poles, S and N. 'prime' is the noun for a prime number.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven has no divisors but one and itself, so it is an example of a prime number.

clue.text: Good people admitting odd sexual preference for lizards

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: SS is saints, good people
a kink is an unusual sexual taste

explanation.surface: Saints confessing a strange fetish for reptiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' looks like confessing but means letting in.
explanation.definitionFit: These smooth-scaled reptiles with short legs are a family of lizard.

clue.text: Unlimited underwear for £1

indicators.note: without limits the first and last letters go

parts.note: knickers are underpants

explanation.surface: Bargain underwear on sale for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlimited' removes the end letters of KNICKERS.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a pound sterling, as in 'it cost me twenty quid' said with this word.

clue.text: Ask Piers to dance, socialising in Davos?

indicators.note: letters made to dance jump about into a new order

explanation.surface: Inviting Piers onto the floor at a Swiss resort party.
explanation.walkthrough: Davos is a Swiss ski resort; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening drinks and parties after a day on the slopes are the social life of a ski resort like Davos.

clue.text: Drink and fall over, inwardly fit for nothing

indicators.note: one letter put in for another replaces it

parts.note: to topple is to fall over
O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: taking a word inwardly means its middle letter

explanation.surface: Someone who drinks, falls over, and is fit for nothing after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inwardly fit' is the middle letter I of fit, which replaces the O ('nothing') in TOPPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A favourite alcoholic drink is one's usual tipple, a colloquial noun for a drink.

clue.text: Four-line whips, highly toxic stuff

indicators.note: whipping something stirs it up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A parliamentary four-line whip, worse than the usual three-line, is poison for MPs.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-line whip is the strictest instruction to UK MPs to vote with their party; a four-line one is a joke escalation.
explanation.definitionFit: The pale yellow halogen gas is extremely poisonous and reactive, a chemical example of a toxic substance.

clue.text: Draw king and the rest in silence

indicators.note: these pieces go in another word

parts.note: sh is the call for silence
K is the chess abbreviation for king
etc, et cetera, means and the rest

explanation.surface: An art class quietly drawing a king and the rest of the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests a tie or a raffle, but is the verb for making a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a quick rough picture with a pencil is a synonym for draw.

clue.text: James, say, is terrifically entertaining writer

indicators.note: the words are entertaining the answer, holding it inside them

explanation.surface: Praise for Henry James as a terrifically entertaining author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertaining' looks like praise but means holding: the answer is held across 'James, say, is terrifically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who writes short prose pieces on a subject is a kind of author.

clue.text: Doctor Hill retires after onset of yucky fungal infection

indicators.note: one piece placed after another comes later in the answer
the onset is the start, the first letter
a word that retires goes back, so it is read in reverse

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Doctor Hill steps down after catching something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Hill looks like a name; 'retires' reverses TOR (a hill) and it follows Y from 'onset of yucky'.
explanation.definitionFit: This fungus decays timber in buildings, a kind of fungal rot infecting wood.
